title: Best Dog Food (2026)
summary: Consumer Reports and The Clean Label Project evaluated dog foods for nutrient consistency and contaminant levels, identifying specific brands that meet safety and nutritional standards.
method: Picks were selected based on recommendations from Consumer Reports, which tested 58 dog foods for nutrients and contaminants, and The Clean Label Project, which analyzed 79 products for contaminant levels. Products appearing in both sources were prioritized.
assumptions: No prices are listed in the provided sources. Availability and specific formulation details may vary by region.

products.name: Hill's Science Diet
why: Consumer Reports tested Hill's Science Diet among 58 dog foods and found that most products, including this brand, did well in meeting recommendations for nutrients like fat, protein, vitamin D, and copper. The testing highlighted significant variation in nutrient levels across different foods, making this brand a reliable choice for consistent nutrition.

The Clean Label Project included Hill's Science Diet in its analysis of 79 products. It appears in the list of products with the lowest levels of contaminants, specifically noting variants like Small & Mini, Sensitive Stomach & Skin, Perfect Weight, and Puppy Premium. This dual recognition supports its safety and quality profile.
products.desc: Hill's Science Diet is a dry dog food brand with multiple formulas including Small & Mini, Sensitive Stomach & Skin, Perfect Weight, and Puppy Premium. It is formulated to meet recommendations for key nutrients such as fat, protein, vitamin D, and copper. The sources do not specify if it is grain-free or list specific ingredient exclusions.
products.benefit: Picture a dog owner checking the label for consistent protein and vitamin D levels before buying a new bag. Hill's Science Diet offers verified nutrient consistency and low contaminant levels, which are key factors in the Consumer Reports and Clean Label Project evaluations. It beats other picks by being explicitly named in both major testing reports for safety and nutrition. The catch: The sources note significant variation in nutrient levels across dog foods in general, so owners must still match the specific formula to their dog's needs.
